title: Jewish groups back stronger measures on Israel in letter to Andy Burnham
summary:
Jewish groups back stronger measures on Israel in letter to Andy Burnham

Submitted by Imran Mulla on Fri, 09/04/2026 - 14:46
Letter to the PM, seen by MEE, argues there is 'a wide diversity of views on Israel among Jewish people in the UK'
Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham meets with Jewish community leaders inside 10 Downing Street in central London on 3 September 2026 (AFP)
Off

Leading members of Jewish civil society groups have written to British Prime Minister Andy Burnham urging him to adopt stronger measures on Israel and "oppose any further attempts to muzzle the Palestine marches".

This comes as the Burnham government prepares to announce a raft of new measures on the occupied West Bank, including a ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements.

Major British Jewish organisations, including the Jewish Leadership Council and the Board of Deputies of British Jews, urged the government not to impose a ban on settlement goods earlier this week and met Burnham in Downing Street.

UK Chief Rabbi Ephraim Mirvis said on Monday that he had met Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and warned sanctions on Israel would have a "negative impact" on British Jews.

But on Thursday, leading members of Holocaust Survivors and Descendants against Gaza Genocide (HSD), Jewish Voice for Liberation (formerly Jewish Voice for Labour) and Jews for Justice for Palestinians, sent a letter to the prime minister arguing the opposite.

Signatories of the letter include Stephen Kapos and Agnes Kory, who are Holocaust survivors.

Seen by MEE, the letter says: "There are several Jewish 'communities' and a wide diversity of views on Israel among Jewish people in the UK and we trust that you will meet with us and other members of the Jewish Bloc in the near future."

The letter also says: "We eagerly await your premiership in the light of your recent call for stronger action against Israel, along with your apology for the Labour Government's slowness to call for a ceasefire."

The signatories explain in the letter that they regularly march "along with the large Jewish Bloc on the Palestine Marches in support of Palestinians in Gaza, calling out what we firmly believe has become a clear case of genocide".

They criticise the characterisation of pro-Palestine marches as antisemitic, saying hostility "has come not from our fellow pro-Palestinian protesters, from whom we have received only goodwill and support, but from the pro-Israel counter-demonstrators".

'Many Jews feel this anger and misery too'

The letter also refers to a previous letter signed by 44 Holocaust survivors and descendants of Holocaust survivors to Burnham's predecessor, Keir Starmer, in May.

That letter urged Starmer not to impose restrictions on pro-Palestine marches after the then-prime minister had suggested he would support restrictions on repeat marches in response to the antisemitic stabbing of two Jewish men in Golders Green, an area of northwest London with a large Jewish population. 

'We are not given any audience by the government, unlike the Jewish establishment bodies which are regularly welcomed in Whitehall'

– Jenny Manson, co-chair of Jewish Voice for Liberation

The signatories argued that pro-Palestine marches, which they took part in, were not linked to the antisemitic attacks.

Sarah Jones, then the minister for policing and crime, sent a reply to the letter, seen by MEE, noting that the "right to peaceful protest is a vital part of our democracy".

However, Jones defended "strengthened police powers to impose conditions on intimidatory protests near places of worship, and a new duty on senior officers to consider the cumulative impact of repeated protest activity when determining whether to impose conditions".

The letter to Burnham this week urges the new prime minister to "oppose any further attempts to muzzle the Palestine marches".

It criticises Labour's "treatment of allegations of antisemitism" under Starmer's leadership, which "resulted in around 70 Jewish members of the Party being accused in some way of antisemitism".

UK to lay out 'measures' against Israel over West Bank settlements
Read More »

The letter says this "has given Israel a protective cloak around the brutality of its actions" and "has undermined the right to freedom of speech and the right to protest".

MEE has contacted Downing Street for comment.

Jenny Manson, a co-chair of Jewish Voice for Liberation, who left the Labour Party last year, told MEE: "We ask that Andy Burnham recognise that the mass marches in support of Gaza are a legitimate expression of the widespread horror felt in Britain at Israel's war crimes and ethnic cleansing in Gaza and the West Bank.

"Many Jews feel this anger and misery too," Manson said.

"Generally, the diversity of Jewish communities and Jewish views is largely ignored. We are not given any audience by the government, unlike the Jewish establishment bodies which are regularly welcomed in Whitehall."

She added: "And as to the message of the marchers, we ask that Burnham hears and responds positively to the marchers' demand, to immediately stop arming Israel."

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced last month that the government would unveil "measures" against Israel over the new E1 settlement project east of Jerusalem that would effectively cut the occupied West Bank in two.

Chief Rabbi Mirvis said earlier this week after the meeting with Miliband: "I told the foreign secretary that many within the UK Jewish community will view such measures with deep dismay, at a time when the vilification of Jews, Judaism and the Jewish State has already reached unprecedented levels."

The Board of Deputies said in a statement after meeting Burnham that sanctions on Israeli settlements risk "harming the legitimate connection between British Jews and places of great religious and cultural significance".

However, Na'amod, an anti-occupation Jewish group, this week expressed support for stronger measures on Israel, calling them the "minimum response" to Israel's actions in the occupied West Bank.

title: Revealed: Microsoft signed $125m contract with Israel during first year of Gaza war
summary:
Revealed: Microsoft signed $125m contract with Israel during first year of Gaza war

Submitted by Sebastian Shehadi on Fri, 09/04/2026 - 15:07
The tech giant did not confirm what services were provided to the Israeli defence ministry in the contract
The logo of Microsoft displayed on the facade of the company's French headquarters in Issy-les-Moulineaux, on the outskirts of Paris, on 24 April 2026 (AFP)
Off

Microsoft signed a contract worth more than $100m with the Israeli government in 2024, according to documents published on the Israeli Ministry of Finance’s Hebrew-language website, Middle East Eye can reveal.

The multimillion-dollar deal appears in Israel's annual budget-execution report for 2024, which was published by the finance ministry's accountant general in March 2025.

However, details of the Microsoft agreement were obscured within a lengthy list of procurement commitments and only surfaced following close analysis of the budget report by MEE.

Buried in the report is a list of the defence ministry's largest procurement commitments. One entry records an agreement signed in 2024 with Microsoft "for the purchase of software licensing", worth approximately 464 million shekels (about $125.4m).

According to the document, the full value of the contract remained outstanding as of 31 December 2024 – meaning nothing had been paid that year – and the engagement is expected to conclude in 2027.

The report does not disclose what software the agreement covers, which bodies or units within Israel’s defence ministry or armed forces would use it, or whether the 2027 date refers to the licence term, the payment schedule or both.

Microsoft did not answer questions about the contract, telling MEE it "had nothing to add from our side".

Renewal of previous contract 

Last year, an internal document reviewed by the Associated Press revealed that Microsoft signed a $133m three-year contract with the Israeli military in 2021. The AP also found that Microsoft listed the Israeli military as an "S500" client, a designation reserved for the company's highest-priority customers.

The AP identified at least 635 individual subscriptions held by the Israeli military, under code names including "Mamram" and "8200", the latter referring to an elite Israeli cyberwarfare unit.

Former Microsoft employees who have tracked the tech giant’s Israeli contracts told MEE that the newly identified agreement could be a renewal of the agreement Israel signed with Microsoft in 2021.

Both deals share several features. The earlier contract ran for three years, while the Israeli government documents record a Microsoft agreement beginning in 2024 and running until 2027.

Their reported values are also similar: $133m for the earlier contract and approximately $125.4m for the new one.

The two figures come from different sources, however.

The Israeli budget report does not identify the 2024 agreement with Microsoft as a renewal of a previous one.

What Microsoft cut, and what it kept

The contract signed in 2024 predates the controversy over Microsoft's provision of cloud services to the Israeli military, and the budget document recording it was published months before that period began.

In August 2025, the Guardian, working with +972 Magazine and Local Call, reported that Israel's military surveillance agency, Unit 8200, had used Microsoft's Azure cloud platform to store recordings of millions of phone calls made by Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, with sources saying the database helped shape military operations and prepare air strikes.

Internal documents obtained by the AP show that Microsoft’s global Azure support team responded to approximately 130 direct requests from Israel’s military during the first 10 months of the war.

'This contract is yet another crystal clear evidence of how Microsoft and its executives continue to enable, power, accelerate, and profit from Israel's ongoing crimes against Palestinians'

- Abdo Mohamed, No Azure for Apartheid

The investigation described invoices showing Unit 8200 had paid Microsoft tens of millions of dollars for priority computing resources and technical support across Azure and related AI products – a smaller sum than the licensing engagement recorded in the Israeli budget document, and one billed on a different basis. Cloud services are charged by consumption; the engagement in the budget report is a fixed multi-year commitment.

Microsoft commissioned an external review, conducted by the law firm Covington & Burling. The following month, the company's president, Brad Smith, said Microsoft had "ceased and disabled a set of services to a unit within the Israel Ministry of Defense".

A leaked email seen by the Guardian sent by Smith, who is also Microsoft’s vice-chair, to company employees said the company had “only disabled a small subset of services to only one unit of the Israeli military” without specifying which one.

The budget document, which records the ministry's position as of 31 December 2024 - nine months before the cloud services were disabled - shows no link between the licensing agreement and the products Microsoft cut.

What it does establish, however, is that the licensing agreement was on the ministry's books, unpaid and running to 2027, before the controversy broke. The engagement it records is described as software licensing rather than cloud or AI services – the categories Microsoft said it had disabled.

A long-standing presence

Microsoft has said the bulk of its Israeli military business continues. The company has held large-scale licensing arrangements with Israeli government bodies for more than two decades.

The tech giant also has at least nine Microsoft employees dedicated to serving the Israeli military, according to documents obtained by the AP.

Information posted online showed the team includes a senior executive who spent 14 years in Unit 8200 and a former IT leader for military intelligence.

Its physical presence in the country is substantial. Microsoft runs server farms in two large buildings outside Tel Aviv and a 46,000-square-metre campus in Herzliya, along with an office in Gav-Yam in the south that has flown a large Israeli flag.

Inside the campaign to end Microsoft's collaboration with the Israeli army
Read More »

Microsoft has fired at least nine employees over protests against its business with Israel since October 2024, and more than a dozen have been fired or arrested in total.

Among them was Abdo Mohamed, a data scientist fired by Microsoft after organising a vigil for Palestinians killed in Gaza outside the company's Redmond headquarters. 

Now an organiser with the campaign group No Azure for Apartheid, Mohamed told MEE that the contract demonstrates the company's continuing role in Israel's crimes against Palestine.

"The newly revealed deal cements the active role Microsoft, its technologies and its executives play in powering Israel's apartheid and genocide,” said Mohamed.

"Make no mistake: as Israel intensified its ongoing genocidal and ethnic cleansing campaign all over Palestine in 2023 and 2024, and as workers with our campaign at Microsoft spoke out in protest of its genocide profiteering business, Microsoft executives chose willingly to double down on their complicity in genocide and apartheid by signing this contract worth [over $100m]."

Mohamed said the deal’s timing coincided with a surge in the Israeli military's use of Microsoft's cloud and AI services during the war, which he said reached as much as 200 times pre-October 2023 levels in some cases.

"This contract is yet more crystal-clear evidence of how Microsoft and its executives continue to enable, power, accelerate and profit from Israel's ongoing crimes against Palestinians," added Mohamed.

"That's why our campaign continues to apply pressure until Microsoft puts an end to its genocide-profiteering business with the Israeli military and government."

Marcus Barnett, a spokesperson for the United Tech and Allied Workers (UTAW) section of the UK’s Communication Workers Union (CWU), said tech workers are turning to union organising to exert some influence over the company’s role in the genocide.

'Tech workers haven’t been isolated from the rest of the world witnessing war and genocide dominate the news headlines and our phone screens'

- Marcus Barnett, United Tech and Allied Workers

“Tech workers haven’t been isolated from the rest of the world witnessing war and genocide dominate the news headlines and our phone screens,” said Barnett.

“It’s no surprise that many are turning to workplace organising to assert their humanity, and we urge anyone with real concerns to stand up and form a workplace union to articulate these issues with strength.”

The Microsoft contract is one of 33 defence engagements that the report dates to 2024, collectively worth about $13.6bn.

The overwhelming majority by value are arms and military hardware – fighter aircraft, ammunition, air-defence systems – bought largely from the US government.

Microsoft is among a small number of non-hardware contracts. The report does not describe the Microsoft engagement as war-related. Only one of the 33 contracts from that year carries an explicit reference to the war in the ministry's own text. The others are identified here by their recorded date alone, in a year when Israel was conducting a genocidal war.

Israel's defence ministry buys a wide range of goods and services that are not weapons, and a licensing renewal may be routine procurement unconnected to the conduct of the war.

MEE contacted the Israeli government and Israeli embassy in the UK for comment, but received no response.

Israel's genocide in Gaza
Areeb Ullah

title: Security Vulnerability in a Voting System
summary:
It’s a vulnerability that allows someone to recover the order of ballots cast, newly exploited with AI tools.

Nearly four years since the original vulnerability was disclosed, I was still able to use it to analyze voter behavior in Georgia (one of the 21 states that uses affected scanners) in the recent May 2026 primary.

Notably, I never touched a voting machine, exploited a network, examined source code, or accessed anything non-public.

After pointing a coding agent to the original vulnerability paper, I supplied it with two data sources highlighted in the paper: the early-voting list for each county, and the “CVR” (cast-vote record) file, containing every ballot and its selections (but not the voters’ names or other identifying information). The CVR file is available upon request, precisely because a public, ballot-level record is what makes election results independently verifiable...

title: AI Coding Agents Are Installing Unknown/Untrusted Code on Corporate Networks
summary:
We cannot forget that AI coding agents are not yet trustworthy:

Researchers at a stealth startup in Israel scanned 6,214 live domains belonging to defense contractors, Fortune 500, and Big Tech companies. Of the 8,265 llms.txt and llms-full.txt files they found (many sites hosted both an llms.txt and an llms-full.txt file), 120 of them, each on a different site, pointed to one or more code packages or domain names that weren’t registered. To test what happens when an AI agent processes such files, the researchers registered a handful of the unclaimed names and hosted packages that caused any machine executing them to reach out to their server. Within an hour, the researchers received a phone-home response from a Fortune 500 company. Over time, they got a few dozen more, some from more Fortune 500 companies and others from startups. Their beacon also recorded the chain of parent processes that spawned each install, ultimately revealing that coding agents, including Claude, OpenAI’s Codex, and Nous Research’s Hermes, were involved. Anthropic, OpenAI, and Nous Research did not respond to requests for comment by the time of publication...

title: Iranian diplomat warns regional countries over US attacks
summary:
Iranian diplomat warns regional countries over US attacks

Iranian diplomat Mojtaba Ferdowsi Pour has said that countries in the Middle East must not permit the use of their territory and airspace as a launchpad for attacks on Iran.

Speaking to Al Mayadeen, Iran's ambassador to Egypt said that international law prohibited such attacks, which have been launched by the US during the course of the war on Iran. 

Ferdowsi Pour said that Iran's American enemies had not yet understood that the Iranian people were "resistant", and would not surrender. 

Iran's top diplomat in Cairo said relations between Iran and Egypt were moving in the right direction and that there was "continuous communication" between the two countries.

title: UK police raid 84-year-old retired priest's home over activism
summary:
UK police raid 84-year-old retired priest's home over activism

An 84-year-old retired priest known for her climate change and pro-Palestine activism had her home raided by British police on Friday, according to the campaign group Defend Our Juries (DOJ).

Sue Parfitt has in the past shown support for the proscribed direct action group Palestine Action, and attended a peaceful protest on Wednesday with the environmental activist group Just Stop Oil.

DOJ said police had raided Parfitt's home on Friday. Middle East Eye has reported recently on the Palestine Action activists who have had their homes raided by British counter-terrorism police, as well as on the campaigners waiting to have their homes raided.

Pressure is growing on new prime minister Andy Burnham to rescind the ban on Palestine Action, which is eating up vast amounts of police time.
